﴿And the mountains are crumbled to powder⁠﴾. On it there are five opinions:

First: They flow like a flood, as said by Mujahid.

Second: They are demolished with a demolishing, as said by Ikrimah.

Third: They are set in motion, as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and from this is the saying of al-Aghlab al-'Ijli:

We crumbled (them) with a trace that raised (dust),
it lit up five (nights), and then it traveled on.

(p. 447) Fourth: They are cut into pieces, as said by al-Hasan.

Fifth: They are crushed as sawiq (roasted meal) is crushed, meaning moistened. Basisah is the flour that is moistened and taken as provision. A thief from Ghatafan said:

Do not bake bread (for us) and crumble (it) into dust,
and do not delay us with a camel-stop to hold us back.

﴿So they become scattered dust⁠﴾. On it there are four opinions:

First: It is the rising of dust that flies up and then vanishes; so Allah makes their deeds like that, as said by 'Ali.

Second: It is the rays of the sun that come through a window (kuwwah), as said by Mujahid.

Third: It is the fine dust that flies from fire when it is agitated; when it falls it is nothing, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Fourth: It is what dries of the leaves of trees, which the wind scatters, as said by Qatadah.

As for "scattered" (munbaththan), there are three meanings:

First: Dispersed, as said by al-Suddi.

Second: Spread out.

Third: Strewn.

﴿And you were three kinds⁠﴾, meaning three categories. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: two in Paradise and one in the Fire.

On these two there are two interpretations:

First: What Ibn 'Abbas said, that they are those mentioned in the Surah of the Angels (Fatir): ﴿Then We made to inherit the Book those whom We have chosen from Our servants⁠﴾.

Second: What al-Nu'man ibn Bashir narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning ﴿And you were three kinds⁠﴾, the verse.

(p. 448) As for their being made into kinds (azwaj), there are two possible meanings:

First: That this category among them includes those who are abundant (in good deeds) and those who fall short, and so it is a pair (zawj).

Second: That in each category among them there are men and women, and so it is a pair.

﴿So the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?⁠﴾. Concerning them there are five interpretations:

First: The companions of the right hand are those taken from the right side of Adam, and the companions of the left are those taken from the left side of Adam, as said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Second: The companions of the right hand are those given their record in their right hand, and the companions of the left are those given their record in their left hand, as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Third: The companions of the right hand are the people of good deeds, and the companions of the left are the people of evil deeds, as said by Ibn Jurayj.

Fourth: The companions of the right hand are the fortunate ones (al-mayamin) with respect to themselves, and the companions of the left are the unfortunate ones (al-mashaʾim) with respect to themselves, as said by al-Hasan.

Fifth: The companions of the right hand are the people of Paradise, and the companions of the left are the people of the Fire, as said by al-Suddi.

His saying: ﴿And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left?⁠﴾ is to magnify the punishment that they will receive.

﴿And the foremost, the foremost⁠﴾, ﴿those are the ones brought near⁠﴾. Concerning them there are five opinions:

First: They are the prophets, as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Second: They are the foremost to faith from every nation, as said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Third: They are those who prayed toward the two qiblahs, as said by Ibn Sirin.

Fourth: They are the first people to go to the mosques in the early hours and the swiftest of them in hastening in the way of Allah, as said by Uthman ibn Abi Sawadah.

Fifth: They are four: among them is the foremost of the nation of Musa, who is Hizqil, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and the foremost of the nation of 'Isa, who is Habib the carpenter, companion of Antioch; and two from the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), who are Abu Bakr and 'Umar, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

It may also bear a sixth meaning: that they are those who embraced Islam in Makkah before the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration, and in Madinah before his migration to them, because they preceded in Islam before the time of desire and fear (al-raghbah wa al-rahbah).

(p. 449) Concerning the repetition of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost⁠﴾, there are two opinions:

One: The foremost in the world to faith, and the foremost in the Hereafter to Paradise, they are those brought near, as said by al-Kalbi.

Two: It is possible that they are the believers in the prophets of their times, and their foremost in faith are those brought near, the ones placed first among them.

﴿ثُلَّةٌ مِنَ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ (a company of the earlier peoples). In this there are three interpretations:

First: they are the group (al-jama'ah), and from this usage is the verse of the poet:

؎ You are not humbled among your whole clan, whom a company (ثُلَّة) does not seek to overcome.

Second: it means half (al-shatr, al-nisf), as said by al-Dahhak.

Third: it means a band (al-fi'ah), as said by Abu 'Ubaydah, and from this is the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

؎ Leave me to travel through the lands, perhaps I shall meet for Bishr a band (ثُلَّة) of warriors.

Regarding His words ﴿مِنَ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ (from the earlier ones) there are two opinions:

One: they are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by Abu Bakrah.

Two: they are the people of Noah, as said by al-Hasan.

﴿وَقَلِيلٌ مِنَ الآخِرِينَ﴾ (and a few from the later ones). Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: they are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by al-Hasan.

Two: they are those whose Islam came early, before they were fully complete. Abu Hurayrah narrated that when ﴿ثُلَّةٌ مِنَ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ and ﴿وَقَلِيلٌ مِنَ الآخِرِينَ﴾ were revealed, this distressed the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), so the verse was revealed: ﴿ثُلَّةٌ مِنَ الأوَّلِينَ * وَثُلَّةٌ مِنَ الآخِرِينَ﴾ (a company from the earlier ones and a company from the later ones). He, peace be upon him, then said: "I hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise, rather a third of the people of Paradise, rather you will be half of the people of Paradise, and you will share with them in the second half."

﴿عَلى سُرُرٍ مَوْضُونَةٍ﴾ (upon couches interwoven). It means the couches; its singular is sarir, and it was so named because it is a seat of joy (surur).

Regarding al-mawdunah (الموضونة, "interwoven") there are four interpretations:

One: it is that which is joined with gold, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Two: it is that which is closely woven in its weave, as said by al-Dahhak, and from this is the verse of Labid:

؎ If they are alarmed, they will rush with a closely woven (مَوْضُونَة) one, while the white swords flash like stars, their blades.

Three: it is that which is plaited (al-madfurah), as said by Abu Hamzah Ya'qub ibn Mujahid, and from this is the word (وضين) for the saddle-girth of the camel, which is the wide strap plaited from thongs.

Four: it is that whose parts are joined to one another.

﴿يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾ (there will go around them youths made eternal). Al-wildan (الولدان) is the plural of walid, and they are the servants (al-wusafa').

Regarding His words ﴿مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾ (made eternal) there are two opinions:

One: they are adorned (مُسَوَّرُونَ) with bracelets (بالأسورة) and adorned (مُقَرَّطُونَ) with earrings (بالأقراط), as said by al-Farra'. The poet said:

؎ And women adorned with silver (مُخَلَّدات), as if their hips were the sand-dune hills.

Two: they are those who remain at their young age, not dying and not changing, as said by al-Hasan, and from this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

؎ And will anyone be blessed except a happy one made eternal, little troubled by cares, who does not spend the night in worry?

(p-451) It may also admit a third meaning: they are those who remain with them, who do not look at them with disapproval nor turn away from them as they did in the world.

﴿بِأكْوابٍ وأبارِيقَ﴾ (with cups and jugs). Regarding these two there are two opinions:

One: al-akwab (الأكواب) are the cups which have no handles, as said by al-Dahhak.

Two: al-akwab are those whose mouths are round, and al-abariq (الأباريق) are those from which one scoops, as said by Qatadah. The poet said:

؎ They ran at me with a clear wine (قَرْقَف) which pours from their cups.

﴿وَكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ﴾ (and a cup from a flowing spring). Al-ka's (الكأس) is the name of the vessel when there is drink in it, and al-ma'in (المعين) is what flows of water or wine. However, what is meant here is wine. He described the wine as flowing from its spring without pressing, like flowing water.

﴿لا يُصَدَّعُونَ عَنْها﴾ (they will not be affected with headache from it). Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: its meaning is that they will not be prevented from it, as said by Abu Hamzah Ya'qub ibn Mujahid.

Two: they will not be dispersed from it. Ibn Qutaybah related this and cited the verse of the rajiz (poet):

؎ He turned away from him and was split (فانصدع).

Three: no pain of the head, which is headache (al-suda'), will reach them from drinking it, as said by Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

Regarding His words ﴿وَلا يُنْزِفُونَ﴾ (nor will they be exhausted) there are four interpretations:

One: their intellects will not be drained so that they become intoxicated, as said by Ibn Zayd and Qatadah.

Two: they will not grow weary, as said by Ikrimah.

Three: they will not vomit, as said by Yahya ibn Wathhab.

Four: this is the interpretation of the one who read it with a kasrah on the zay (يُنزِفون), meaning their wine will not run out. From this is the verse of al-Ubayrad:

؎ By my life, if you are drained (أنزفتم) or sober, you are indeed a wretched company of drinkers, O family of Abjar.

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "In wine there are four qualities: intoxication, headache, vomiting and urination, and Allah has mentioned the wine of Paradise and cleansed it of these qualities."

﴿وَحُورٌ عِينٌ﴾ (and wide-eyed maidens). Al-hur (الحور) are the white ones, and they were so called for their whiteness. Regarding al-'in (العين) there are two opinions:

One: they are those with large eyes, as the poet said:

؎ When the eyes of women are large, and of other than women they are 'in.

Two: they are those whose black of the eye is intensely dark and whose white of the eye is pure, as the poet said:

؎ When the eye has in it a hawar (a dark-and-white contrast), its sign is whiteness upon blackness.

﴿كَأمْثالِ اللُّؤْلُؤِ المَكْنُونِ﴾ (like pearls well-guarded). Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: in their freshness and the purity of their colours.

Two: they are like pearls in the uniformity of their bodies in beauty from all sides, as the poet said:

؎ As if she was created in the shell of a pearl, every side of her is a face watching over (لمرصاد).

﴿لا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيها لَغْوًا ولا تَأْثِيمًا﴾ (they will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech). Regarding this there are three interpretations:

One: they will not hear in Paradise falsehood or lying, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Two: they will not hear therein contention (khulfan), meaning they will not oppose one another over it as they oppose one another in the world, and they will not sin by drinking it as they sin in the world, as said by al-Dahhak.

Three: they will not hear therein abuse or sin, as said by Mujahid.

It may admit a fourth meaning: they will not hear anything preventing them from it, nor anything reproaching them for drinking it.

﴿إلا قِيلا سَلامًا سَلامًا﴾ (except the saying: "Peace, peace"). Regarding this there are three interpretations:

One: rather they will hear a word of gentle speech and good discourse.

Two: rather they will greet one another with peace, in good manners and noble character.

Three: meaning a word that leads to safety.

It may admit a fourth meaning: that it is said to them, "Congratulations (هنيئا)."

؎ You are not humbled among your whole clan, whom a company (ثُلَّة) does not seek to overcome.

Second: it means half (al-shatr, al-nisf), as said by al-Dahhak.

Third: it means a band (al-fi'ah), as said by Abu 'Ubaydah, and from this is the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

؎ Leave me to travel through the lands, perhaps I shall meet for Bishr a band (ثُلَّة) of warriors.

One: they are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by Abu Bakrah.

Two: they are the people of Noah, as said by al-Hasan.

﴿وَقَلِيلٌ مِنَ الآخِرِينَ﴾ (and a few from the later ones). Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: they are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by al-Hasan.

Two: they are those whose Islam came early, before they were fully complete. He, peace be upon him, then said: "I hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise, rather a third of the people of Paradise, rather you will be half of the people of Paradise, and you will share with them in the second half."

﴿عَلى سُرُرٍ مَوْضُونَةٍ﴾ (upon couches interwoven). It means the couches; its singular is sarir, and it was so named because it is a seat of joy (surur).

Regarding al-mawdunah (الموضونة, "interwoven") there are four interpretations:

One: it is that which is joined with gold, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Two: it is that which is closely woven in its weave, as said by al-Dahhak, and from this is the verse of Labid:

؎ If they are alarmed, they will rush with a closely woven (مَوْضُونَة) one, while the white swords flash like stars, their blades.

Three: it is that which is plaited (al-madfurah), as said by Abu Hamzah Ya'qub ibn Mujahid, and from this is the word (وضين) for the saddle-girth of the camel, which is the wide strap plaited from thongs.

Four: it is that whose parts are joined to one another.

﴿يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾ (there will go around them youths made eternal). Al-wildan (الولدان) is the plural of walid, and they are the servants (al-wusafa').

Regarding His words ﴿مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾ (made eternal) there are two opinions:

One: they are adorned (مُسَوَّرُونَ) with bracelets (بالأسورة) and adorned (مُقَرَّطُونَ) with earrings (بالأقراط), as said by al-Farra'. The poet said:

؎ And women adorned with silver (مُخَلَّدات), as if their hips were the sand-dune hills.

Two: they are those who remain at their young age, not dying and not changing, as said by al-Hasan, and from this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

؎ And will anyone be blessed except a happy one made eternal, little troubled by cares, who does not spend the night in worry?

(p-451) It may also admit a third meaning: they are those who remain with them, who do not look at them with disapproval nor turn away from them as they did in the world.

﴿بِأكْوابٍ وأبارِيقَ﴾ (with cups and jugs). Regarding these two there are two opinions:

One: al-akwab (الأكواب) are the cups which have no handles, as said by al-Dahhak.

Two: al-akwab are those whose mouths are round, and al-abariq (الأباريق) are those from which one scoops, as said by Qatadah. The poet said:

؎ They ran at me with a clear wine (قَرْقَف) which pours from their cups.

﴿وَكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ﴾ (and a cup from a flowing spring). Al-ka's (الكأس) is the name of the vessel when there is drink in it, and al-ma'in (المعين) is what flows of water or wine. However, what is meant here is wine. He described the wine as flowing from its spring without pressing, like flowing water.

﴿لا يُصَدَّعُونَ عَنْها﴾ (they will not be affected with headache from it). Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: its meaning is that they will not be prevented from it, as said by Abu Hamzah Ya'qub ibn Mujahid.

Two: they will not be dispersed from it. Ibn Qutaybah related this and cited the verse of the rajiz (poet):

؎ He turned away from him and was split (فانصدع).

Three: no pain of the head, which is headache (al-suda'), will reach them from drinking it, as said by Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

Regarding His words ﴿وَلا يُنْزِفُونَ﴾ (nor will they be exhausted) there are four interpretations:

One: their intellects will not be drained so that they become intoxicated, as said by Ibn Zayd and Qatadah.

Two: they will not grow weary, as said by Ikrimah.

Three: they will not vomit, as said by Yahya ibn Wathhab.

Four: this is the interpretation of the one who read it with a kasrah on the zay (يُنزِفون), meaning their wine will not run out. From this is the verse of al-Ubayrad:

؎ By my life, if you are drained (أنزفتم) or sober, you are indeed a wretched company of drinkers, O family of Abjar.

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "In wine there are four qualities: intoxication, headache, vomiting and urination, and Allah has mentioned the wine of Paradise and cleansed it of these qualities."

One: they are those with large eyes, as the poet said:

؎ When the eyes of women are large, and of other than women they are 'in.

Two: they are those whose black of the eye is intensely dark and whose white of the eye is pure, as the poet said:

؎ When the eye has in it a hawar (a dark-and-white contrast), its sign is whiteness upon blackness.

﴿كَأمْثالِ اللُّؤْلُؤِ المَكْنُونِ﴾ (like pearls well-guarded). Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: in their freshness and the purity of their colours.

Two: they are like pearls in the uniformity of their bodies in beauty from all sides, as the poet said:

؎ As if she was created in the shell of a pearl, every side of her is a face watching over (لمرصاد).

﴿لا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيها لَغْوًا ولا تَأْثِيمًا﴾ (they will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech). Regarding this there are three interpretations:

One: they will not hear in Paradise falsehood or lying, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Two: they will not hear therein contention (khulfan), meaning they will not oppose one another over it as they oppose one another in the world, and they will not sin by drinking it as they sin in the world, as said by al-Dahhak.

Three: they will not hear therein abuse or sin, as said by Mujahid.

It may admit a fourth meaning: they will not hear anything preventing them from it, nor anything reproaching them for drinking it.

Three: meaning a word that leads to safety.

﴿And the companions of the right hand: what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ On this there are six opinions:

First: they are the people of truth. This was said by al-Suddi.

Second: they are below the rank of those brought near (al-muqarrabun). This was said by Maymun ibn Mihran.

Third: they are those who are given their record in their right hand. This was said by Ya'qub ibn Mujahid.

Fourth: they are the followers in good conduct (al-tabi'un bi-ihsan) from among the nations who did not meet the prophets. This was said by al-Hasan.

Fifth: what Asbat related from al-Suddi: God, exalted is He, wiped the back of Adam and drew out from the right side of his back offspring like specks (dharr), white. He said to them, "Enter Paradise, and I do not care." Then He wiped the left side of his back and drew out offspring like specks, black. He said to them, "Enter the Fire, and I do not care." That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the right hand﴾, and His saying: ﴿and the companions of the left hand﴾.

Sixth: what Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The companions of the right hand are those who mixed a righteous deed with another evil one, then repented after that and set things right." ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾. Al-sidr is the lote-tree (al-nabq). Regarding makhdud (without thorns) there are three opinions:

First: it is the smooth one with no thorns. This was said by Ikrimah, and others said: its lote-fruit has no worms (la 'ujm), it is said "khudidat al-shajara" when the tree has shed its thorns.

Second: it is the one laden with fruit, bent under its load. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: the one whose branches hang low. The lote-tree was singled out for mention because its fruit is the most desired of fruits by souls, in longing for it, and its scent is the sweetest.

﴿And acacia (talh) arranged in tiers﴾. On this there are three opinions: (p-454)

First: that talh is the banana. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan and Ikrimah.

Second: it is a tree found in Yemen and the Hijaz in abundance, called talhah. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn Humayd. It was also said that it is among the most beautiful trees in appearance, so that some of their trees would be for eating and some for beholding. The rajaz-poet said:

"Her guide gave her good news and said: Tomorrow you will see the acacia and the sands (al-ahbal)."

Third: that it is the flower-cluster (al-tal'). This was said by 'Ali, who related that he used to recite: "wa-tal'in mandud". Regarding al-mandud there are two opinions:

One: arranged in rows. This was said by al-Suddi.

The other: piled up. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿And extended shade﴾, i.e., constant.

A second possibility: it is complete.

﴿And water poured out﴾, i.e., flowing without a trench.

Another possibility: it is that which flows over them from ascent and descent, unlike in this world. Al-Dahhak said: from the Garden of Eden to the people of the tents.

﴿And abundant fruit﴾ ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾. This may have two meanings:

One: neither cut off by perishing, nor kept out of reach by thorns or distance.

There is also a third meaning: neither cut off by time, nor forbidden by trees.

﴿And raised couches﴾. On this there are two opinions:

One: they are the cushions spread for sitting and sleeping, raised by the abundance of their stuffing, increasing enjoyment of them.

The other: they are the wives, since a wife is called firash (bed), and from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The child belongs to the bed, and the adulterer gets the stone." This was said by Ibn Bahr.

On this basis there are two possible meanings:

One: they are raised in the hearts because of the intensity of inclination towards them.

The other: they are raised above indecencies and filth.

﴿Indeed We have created them a creation﴾. This means the women of the people of this world. On their creation in Paradise there are two opinions:

One: it means their creation in the graves. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The other: their return after grey hair and old age, as young virgins. This was said by al-Dahhak, and Umm Salamah related it as a marfu' report: ﴿So We made them virgins﴾. On this there are two opinions:

One: maidens after they were not maidens. This was said by Ya'qub ibn Mujahid.

The other: whoever comes to her finds her a virgin. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

A third possibility: virgins among the wives, namely the first ones, because they are sweeter in souls and inclination towards them is stronger, as the poet said:

"Her love came to me before I knew love, and it found a heart empty, and it settled in."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ardan atraban﴾. On this there are seven interpretations:

First: that al-'urub are those who are restrained upon their husbands, who make themselves beloved to them. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi.

Second: that they are those who make themselves beloved to their co-wives, so that they remain in obedience to him and help one another in pleasing him. This was said by Ikrimah.

Third: al-shakalah in the dialect of the people of Makkah, and al-ghanjah in the dialect of the people of Madinah. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and from it is the saying of Labid:

"In the tent is a 'urub, not vulgar, with full hips, the eye is blinded before her."

Fourth: they are those good in speech. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

[Also] (p-456) Fifth: that they are women who love their husbands, because their love for him increases his inclination towards her and his passion for her.

Sixth: that they are those good in their sexual intimacy (husbanding), so that the enjoyment is sweeter.

Seventh: what Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "'Uruban: their speech is Arabic." ﴿Atraban﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: that is, equals in age. This was said by 'Atiyyah.

al-Kalbi said: of one age, thirty-three years. It is said of women atrab, and of men qiran, amthal and ashkal. This was said by Mujahid.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 56, verses 57–62:**

﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ This admits of two meanings:

First: We created your provision, so will you not believe that this is your food?

Second: We created you, so why do you not believe that We will requite you, with reward and punishment, when We bring you back?

﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ This means the drop of semen (*mani*). Al-Farra' said: it is said *amna* (أمْنى) *yumni* and *mani* (مَنِيَ) *yamni*, with the same meaning.

In my view, it is also possible that their meanings differ: *amna* (أمْنى) is used when one ejaculates from intercourse, and *mani* (مَنِيَ) when it is from a wet dream (*ihtilam*).

There are two explanations for why it is called *mani* (مَنِيّ):

First: because it is poured out (*imna'*), that is, shed.

Second: because it is measured (*taqdir*). From this comes *al-mina'* (المِناء), the measure by which things are weighed, since it is a fixed quantity; likewise *mani* is a precise quantity for shaping the creation.

﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creators?﴾ This admits of two meanings:

First: That is, We created a human being (*basharan sawiyyan*) from the despised semen, and this is stated as a favour (*imtinan*).

Second: We created a human being from what you have witnessed of semen, so We are more capable of creating what is hidden, that is, your restoration. This is stated as proof (*burhan*), because they acknowledge it under the first meaning, but deny it under the second.

﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ has three meanings:

First: We have decreed death upon you (*qada*).

Second: We have prescribed death for you (*kataba*).

Third: We have made death equal among you (*sawwa*).

If the first meaning is taken, with the sense of *qada*, there are two explanations: (p-٤٥٩) first, He decreed annihilation and then requital; second, that sons might succeed fathers.

If the second meaning is taken, with the sense of *kataba*, there are two explanations:

First: We wrote its quantity, so it neither increases nor decreases. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

Second: We wrote its time, so it neither precedes nor follows it. This was said by Mujahid.

If the third meaning is taken, with the sense of *sawwa*, there are two explanations:

First: We made equal the obedient and the disobedient.

Second: We made equal the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿Nor are We to be outdone﴾ has two meanings:

First: We are not outdone in what We have decreed of death among you, so that you do not die.

Second: We are not outdone in your being made to increase its quantity or to delay it from its time.

The second interpretation is that this is the beginning of a new statement, which is connected to what follows it in the words of the Exalted: ﴿on condition that We replace your likenesses and bring you into being in what you do not know﴾. On this, its interpretation has two meanings:

First: Since We were not outdone in creating others like you, so We are not incapable of changing your states after your death.

Second: Just as We were not incapable of creating others like you, so We are not incapable of changing your states after your death, just as We were not incapable of changing them during your life.

According to this interpretation, there is an implied, omitted element in the statement; according to the first interpretation, the whole of it is explicit.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 56, verse 63–74:

﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ and so on.

He attributed the sowing (al-harth) to them and the growing (al-zar') to Himself, the Exalted, because sowing is their action and proceeds according to their choice, whereas growth is from the act of Allah and sprouts according to His choice, not theirs. Likewise is what has been related from the Prophet ﷺ: "Let none of you say 'I have planted' (zara'tu), but let him say 'I have tilled' (harathtu)." This verse contains two matters:

The first: a reminder of favour upon them, in that He caused their crop to grow so that they might live by it, that they may thank Him for His blessing upon them.

The second: a proof that calls for reflection, that when He caused their crop to grow after its seeds had disintegrated and passed into a state of rectification, [from rot to arrangement], until it became a green crop, then made it strong and robust, many times what it had been, then He is more worthy and more capable of restoring those who have died. In this proof there is a sufficient persuasion for those with sound natures.

Then His saying, ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it debris (huṭāman)﴾ means the crop. Ḥuṭām is dried, withered stalks that are destroyed and of no benefit. By this He alerted to two matters:

The first: the blessings He has bestowed upon them in their crop, since He did not make it debris so that they would give thanks.

The second: that they may take a lesson from this within themselves, for just as He makes the crop debris if He wills, so He destroys them if He wills, so that they may take heed and refrain.

﴿So you would be left wondering (tafakkahūna)﴾ after the crop has become debris. Regarding it there are four interpretations:

The first: you would regret (tandamūna). This is the saying of al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, and it is said that it is the dialect of ʿUkl and Tamīm.

The second: you would grieve (taḥzanūna). Said by Ibn Kaysān.

The third: you would blame one another (tulāwimūna). Said by ʿIkrimah.

(p-461) The fourth: you would be amazed (taʿjabūna). Said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

And if this befalls you regarding the destruction of your crop, what befalls you regarding the destruction of your own selves would be greater.

﴿Indeed we are burdened with debt (lamughramūna)﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations:

The first: we are punished (lamuʿadhdhabūna). Said by Qatādah, and from it is the saying of Ibn al-Muhallam:

Your trust that my guarding of you is a disposition, and that my heart is afflicted by you, enamoured (mughram).

The second: we are infatuated with (muwallaʿūna bina). Said by ʿIkrimah, and from it is the saying of al-Namir ibn Tawlab:

He forgot her remembrance by concealment, and he had been a captive (rahīnan) of her, enamoured (mughraman).

That is, infatuated (muwalla').

The third: we are deprived of good fortune (maḥrūmūna min al-ḥaẓẓ). Said by Mujāhid, and from it is the saying of the poet:

The day of al-Nisār and the day of al-Jifār, they were torment and they were passion (gharām).

﴿Have you considered the fire that you kindle (tūrūna)?﴾ That is, you extract it with your firestriker from wood, iron or stone. From it is the saying of the poet:

Indeed fire is kindled by two firesticks, and indeed evil is preceded by speech.

﴿Is it you who produced its tree (ashja-harā)?﴾ That is, you took its root.

﴿Or are We the producers?﴾ meaning the originators.

﴿We made it a reminder (tadhkira)﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations:

The first: a reminder of the [Hereafter's] great fire, said by Qatādah.

The second: an insight for people out of darkness, said by Mujāhid.

﴿And a provision for the travellers (lil-muqwīn)﴾. Regarding it there are five sayings:

The first: a benefit for travellers, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is said of travellers when they alight in the qiyy, which is the barren land in which there is nothing.

The second: those who take enjoyment, both resident and traveller, said by Mujāhid.

The third: for the hungry, in preparing their food, said by Ibn Zayd.

The Arabs say "qad aqwā al-rajul" when his wealth has gone, said al-Nābighah:

By it the riding party is reduced until nothing remains for them except the firestriker and the arrow-shaft of the people, kindled.

The fifth: that the muqwī is the one of abundant wealth, derived from strength (quwwa), so that the rich and the poor both benefit from it.

**The first:** They are their risings and settings. This is the view of Mujahid.

**The third:** The positions of the stars are the sky. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

**The fourth:** The positions of the stars are the *anwa'* (rain-stars, the star-risings by which people attributed rainfall), which the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era) would say, when they were given rain: "We have been given rain by such-and-such a star-rising." God sent them down from the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) in the highest heaven to the noble scribes (*al-Safara al-Kiram*) in the lowest heaven. Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 56, verses 83–87:

﴿Then why, if you are not to be brought to account,﴾ there are seven interpretations concerning it:

First: "not subject to reckoning" (ghayr muhasabin). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: "not to be resurrected" (ghayr mabʿuthin). This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: "not believing" (ghayr musaddiqin). This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Fourth: "not subdued" (ghayr maqhurin). This was said by Maymun ibn Mihran.

Sixth: "not to be recompensed for your deeds" (ghayr majziyyina bi-aʿmalikum). This was related by al-Tabari.

Seventh: "not owned" (ghayr mamlukin). This was said by al-Farra'.

﴿You would return it﴾ meaning: return the soul after death to the body, if you are truthful that you are not guilty.
